CRINE.
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 23.—James Thorp workman in the machine shops, shot and killed Fred Perry a negro, yesterday, attempting to throw stones during an alteration with him. He was arrested. Van Koltz brothers Saturday night shot and killed Henry Stock, at Pleasant Hill. Stock had ordered them out of the store and began firing at them. They have the sympathy of the citizens. ACCIDENTAL SHOOTING.
|Special Telegram to the Globe.|
ACCIDENTAL SHOOTING.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

FARIBAULT, Aug. 23.—Barney Wichers, a young man just 20 years of age, son of Anton Wichers, of this city, was out hunting on East Prairie to-day and while he was putting his gun into the wagon it was accidentally discharged, the entire load passing through the left leg a little below the hip, severing the femoral artery. He was put in the wagon and driven home as fast as possible and Drs. Rose and Wood summoned, who did all in their to save him, but all to no avail. He died in about an hour after reaching home and an hour and a half after the accident. Barney was a promising young man, a general favorite with all. For several years past and up to the time of his death he was head clerk in the dry goods house of J. W. Kollmann, in this city. His life could have undoubtedly have been saved if it had not been for the gross carelessness of his friends who through their excitement did nothing towards staying the flow of blood. Notice of the funeral will appear hereafter.

DEFAULTING POSTMASTER.

DEADWOOD, D. T., Aug. 23.—The jury in the case of ex-Postmaster R. O. Adams, charged with the embezzlement of nearly $12,000, brought in a verdict of guilty. Adams will probably give bail and appeal the case to the territorial supreme court.

KANSAS CITY TRAGEDIES.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 23.—Jas. Thorp, a workman in the Missouri Pacific railroad machine shops, had an altercation yesterday, with Alfred Perry, a negro, and after the latter had made, or attempted to make an assault on him with rocks, shot him four times killing him almost instantly. Thorp was arrested.

Wm. and Robert Van Hultz, brothers, while in the store of Henry Stock, at Pleasant Hill, Saturday night, purchasing provisions, was ordered out of the store by the clerk, who at the same moment fired at them with a pistol. The Van Hultz brothers returned the fire, killing Stock and severely wounding another man named Alexander. The Van Hultz brothers surrendered to officers and have the sympathy of the citizens.

HELD TO ANSWER.

New York, Aug. 23.—James Alliger, broker, has been held in $10,000 bonds to answer the charge of negotiating stolen bonds.

COOPER'S STRIKE.

CINCINNATI, Aug. 23.—Nearly all the coopers of this city joined in a strike this morning for an advance of 15 per cent. in their wages.

A COLORED AFFAIR.

BURMINGHAM, Kansas, Aug. 23.—Thomas Smith and Wesley Thomas, negroes, quarrelled last night in front of W. M. Baker's saloon, and Smith sent a ball through Thomas' lung. A second shot fired by Smith passed through the window of the saloon and struck Baker in the breast. Thomas died in a few minutes and Baker is mortally wounded. Cause, Smith too intimate with Thomas' wife.

THE MAY'S LANDING DISASTER.

PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 23.—The coroner's inquest at May's Landing was concluded today. The jury, in their verdict, say the people killed came to their death from a collision which might have been prevented if Engineer Aitken and Conductor Hoagland had more carefully observed the rules and regulations of the company governing the running of trains.

HELD WITHOUT BAIL.

Ann Matilda Faulkner, a young and prepossessing lady, was found Saturday in the deserted rooms of Hattie Mack. on West Madison street, the body being well decomposed at the time. Clues were followed up, and Dr. Thomas H. Cream and Hattie Mack were arrested on suspicion of producing an abortion and causing the death. At the coroner's inquest to-day revolting details were brought out, but each of the accused attempted to fasten the guilt on the other. The jury held both without bail on the charge of murder.

INHUMAN TREATMENT.

READING, Pa., Aug. 23.—A great sensation has been caused throughout Bucks county by the discovery of Benjamin Zechlor, a lunatic, who had been confined in a house in Albany township, by his brother, Jacob Zechlor, for twenty-seven years. He was chained to the floor, in a small house built specially for him, in a room about eight feet square, with only one window for ventilation.

DOUBLE SHOOTING AND ARSON.

MADISON, Aug. 23.—The house of Martin Winick, on the line between Dane and Columbia counties, was discovered in flames Sunday night, and neighbors forcing an entrance found the body of Mrs. Winick riddled with shot, lying in a pool of blood, and the body of her husband was found on the bed bleeding from two ghastly wounds. The bodies were taken out of the burning house, though somewhat scorched. Winick and wife lived unhappily on account of children of each by former marriages, and it is supposed the old man shot his wife with a shot gun, set fire to the house, then shot himself with a revolver and failing to finish himself discharged the other barrel of the shot gun into his own body. They leave several grown children who live in the neighborhood of the crime.

A BAD FALL.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 23.—J. C. Miller, one of the proprietors of the Daily Critic, whilst adjusting the sash of a third story window this afternoon, lost his balance and fell to the ground, a distance of forty-five feet. He was badly injured and is not expected to recover.

CHILD BURNING.

NEW YORK, Aug. 23.—The police to-night arrested Mrs. Josephine Scheideler, who keeps a candy store at 214 Christie street, and Augusta Wohlrap, midwife, 184 Ludlow street, charged with burning the body of a still born child whose birth was not reported to the health board. It is alleged the child was born a week ago, and that it was burned on Wednesday last.

CRUSHED BY A GUN.

AN ANGRY MOB. Special Dismiss to The Chambers
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 23.—A mob of over 1,000 half-drunken, howling negroes made a bold attempt to lynch one John Moffatt, brother-in-law of Alfred Thorp, who murdered the colored man Perry on Sunday down in West Kansas. This afternoon during the funeral services over Perry's body, it was reported that Moffatt made some foul remark, and the colored folks forgot the funeral and started in pursuit of Moffatt, who fled with a pistol in each hand. The mob chased him nearly ten blocks, throwing brickbats and stones, but he kept them at a distance until the police arrived, who had a hard struggle to keep him from the enraged negroes. During the chase through the streets several pistol-shots were fired by Moffatt, and it was strangened one was killed. The trouble took place near the large packing-houses, and over 200 butchers turned out and threatened to drive every negro into the Missouri River. Serious trouble is yet anticipated, and a large force of police guard the locality.

NEWS SUMMARY.
Accident on a Long Branch Railroad - A Big Batch of Shocking Crimes - Sickness of Prominent Men.
Accident on a Long Branch Railroad — A Big Batch of Shocking Crimes — Sickness of Prominent Men.

The fast newspaper train from New York for Long Branch collided with a train of empty passenger cars near the Long Branch station yesterday morning. The side of one car of the news train was torn away and two other cars were wrecked. Three young men were severely injured, one of whom, Jeremiah Culliland, is in a critical condition. The disaster is ascribed to the carelessness of John Erickson, engineer.

At Pleasant Hill, Mo., on Saturday night, William and Robert Van Holtz, brothers, while buying provisions in the store of Henry Stock, were ordered out by Stock, who, at the same moment fired a pistol at them. They returned the fire killing Stock and severely wounding another man, named Alexander, and then surrendered themselves to the police.

The house of Martin Weinrich, on the line between Dane and Columbia counties, in Wisconsin, was discovered on fire last Sunday night. The door being forced, the bodies of Weinrich and his wife, bearing fatal shot wounds, were found within. The couple had lived unhappily, and it is supposed Weinrich shot his wife and then committed suicide.

Frank Stillwell was shot dead by George Glass on Saturday night while attempting to force an entrance into the latter's house, a disreputable place in Urbana, Ill. Stillwell had been drinking. He leaves a wife and child.

Thomas Smith and Wesley Thomas, negroes, quarrelled in Burlingame, Kansas, on Sunday night, and Thomas was killed. A second shot, fired by Smith, passed through the window of a saloon and mortally wounded a man named Baker.

Michael Wood was arrested in the act of setting fire to a building in College Point, L. I., last Saturday night. Seven incendiary fires have lately occurred in this place, and it is believed that all can be traced to him.

John Dismen was found dead on the stoop of his house at Red Bank, N. J., yesterday morning. While helplessly drunk he had fallen flat on his face with his arms beneath him, and been smothered to death. He was 45 years of age.

The report of the robbery on a Third avenue car in New York is contradicted by the police of that city. They say the affair was nothing more than a disturbance made by two drunken men, who refused to pay their fare to the conductor.

The quarterly interest on the four- and a half per cent. loan, due September 1st, will aggregate $2,800,000. Checks for the payment of the interest on the registered bonds will be sent out by the U. S. Treasurer in a few days.

Mrs. Moles, aged 50 years, was found hanging to a tree near Wheeling, W. Va., on Saturday night. It is supposed she committed suicide to escape "family jars."

The trial at Deadwood of R. O. Adams, for embezzling nearly $12,000, has resulted in his conviction. It is thought he will give bail and appeal the case to the Territorial Supreme Court.

J. C. Miller, one of the proprietors of the Daily Critic, in Washington, D. C., was severely if not fatally injured yesterday, by falling from a third-story window.

Joseph Willner, aged 55 years, committed suicide in Troy, N. Y., on Sunday morning. He has been suffering from sickness, which, it was supposed, had effected his mind.

A telegram from Montrose, Pa., says Warren has been convicted of murder in the second degree. The jury were out thirty-nine hours.

A jewelry store in Danbury, Conn., was robbed of about $500 worth of property by three burglars a few nights ago.

General Albert J. Myer, chief of the Signal Service, remains in a precarious condition at Buffalo. His death was momentarily expected last night.

The condition of Washington McLean, sick at Long Branch, was further improved yesterday, but is still considered critical.

Alfred Terry, colored, was shot dead by James Thorp, in a quarrel, at Kansas City, on Sunday.

John Smithwrite, fireman on the propeller Canistor, was fatally shot by Francis Trainor, in Buffalo, last night. Trainor escaped.

General Grant and party left Denver, Col., yesterday for the East. The General will go directly to Galena.

THE CRIMINAL CALENDAR.
A Springfield, Ky., dispatch says James McHvey was shot and killed by T. R. Phelps, representative of Washington county, on the 26th inst. It was an old feud. Phelps surrendered to the authorities.

A dispatch from Paris states Miss Candace M. Olney, once a well-known New York mulliner, and who was witness in the celebrated Newell divorce suit in April last, killed herself in the Hotel de France, at Pau.

Roland Rucker cheated the gallows at Palestine, Texas, on the 27th inst., by cutting the arteries in one of his wrists and bleeding to death. He was to be hanged on the 28th for the murder of P. Grayson and wife.

Allen Wright (colored) was hanged for the murder of Jesse Wicks, at Dallas, Texas, on the 27th inst. At Waco, in the same state, on the same day, Lynchfield Burke was hanged for the murder of Sarah McBee, aged nine years. He died protesting his innocence.

Four disguised white men molested a negro's cabin near Cochran, Ga., on the night of the 25th inst., when the occupant, John Brown, showed up and with a shot gun killed two brothers named Dykes, blowing the tops of their heads off.

The body of the wife of Wm. Curtis a canal boatman was found in a secluded ravine near Sidney, O., on the 25th inst. They were married in January last but she has been living in Taylorsville, above Dayton, for some time. He went after her with a buggy, on the 25th inst., and on their return he committed the murder. Her trunk, his bloody shirt and a rubber overcoat were found hid under a pile of wood on a canal boat. Curtis is under arrest.

Richard O. Adams. Deadwood's defaulting postmaster, escaped jail on the 24th. A large reward is offered for his capture.

A young woman giving her name as Kate B. Schofield, who took passage from New York on the steamer Arizona, jumped overboard in the Irish channel on the 11th inst., and was drowned. She was 22 years of age, refined and handsome, and lived in the west. Her name is withheld.

Ettie A. Carl is the latest victim of Chicago abortionists. Her body was found in a hallway on West Madison street on the night of the 23d inst., and Dr. Earl, notorious for his conviction and imprisonment for a similar practice, whose office was in the building, was arrested. He confessed having performed the operation which caused the girl's death.

At Salamanaca, N. Y., on the 24th inst., while John Lock Warwick was in a saloon with Mrs. Bohn, alias Lizzie Jackson, who had become enarmored of him and followed him from Syracuse, Fred. Jackson, Lizzie's reputed husband, appeared and fired on the twain, shooting Warrick fatally through the windpipe and seriously wounding the woman. Warwick fired several shots at Jackson but failed to him. All the parties are colored.

The much sought Dr. Buchanan, of bogus medical diploma notoriety, whose disappearance from Philadelphia and supposed drowning from a ferry boat has already been telegraphed over the country, has been run down at last. He was found at Windsor, Ont., opposite Detroit, where he was registered as Mr. Farchild.

Rosario Mell, the Sicilian brigand and member of the society La Maffia, who was sent to the penitentiary at San Francisco for robbery, was pardoned by the governor on the 23d inst., and immediately started by overland train en route to Italy, in charge of an Italian official and Capt. Stone, of the San Francisco police. He was wanted at home for murder, and was pardoned for his offense here in order to admit of his extradition.

The bodies of Simon Zimmerman and his wife were found early on the evening of the 23d instant, at their residence on Clybourn avenue, Chicago, with bullet holes in their heads, which had evidently been made by the husband the night previous. Two children, aged three years and one year, had been in the house all day with the bodies. No cause is assigned for the crime.

THOMAS SMITH and Wesley Thomas (negroes) quarrelled on the 22d inst., in front of W. M. Baker's saloon, Burlingame, Ks., and Smith sent a bail through Thomas' lung. A SANTA FE dispatch says Charles Williams and Louis A. Gaines were hanged at that place on the 21st, for murder. Both died without a struggle, their necks being broken.

In a melee caused by the meeting of a Democratic and Greenback procession at Coffeeville, Yallabusha county, Miss., R. N. Pearson, Greenback candidate for sheriff, shot and badly wounded a negro named Thos. Spearman, and was in turn shot down and seriously wounded by Spearman's friends. Two others were wounded in the fray.

A DISPATCH from Marietta, O., dated the 22d inst., says: "People of the town of Lowel, ten miles distant, on the Muskingum river, were horrified to find yesterday morning that the twin children of Jno. Farley had been drowned in a tub of water during the night. The father and mother were arrested. The children were only a month old. The parents are very poor, and Farley is given to drink. They both deny the crime, but Farley says he believes the wife drowned the babies."

A CHAMPAIGN (Ill.) dispatch of the 22d inst., says: "About 11 o'clock last night Geo. Glass, keeper of a low brothel at Urbana, shot and killed Frank Stillman, a laborer, who was trying to gain forcible admission to Glass' house."

A GENERAL disturbance took place at Morris-town, Tenn., on the 20th instant, between drunken men who were there to attend the circus, and the officers of the law. The town marshal, Jos. B. Morris, and R. T. Richardson, were killed outright, and Sheriff Loop dangerously wounded.

A young woman named Faulkener, from Ottawa, Canada, fell a victim to an abortionist at Chicago on the 20th instant. Dr. Thomas N. Cream and Mrs. Hattie Mackey, a colored woman, are under arrest and mutually accuse each other.

WILLIAM and JOHN LITTLEFIELD, prominent and wealthy stockmen, were killed in a fight at Leesville, Texas, with families named Finney and Martin. An old feud.

A butcher boy named Sevinger was killed at New York city, on the 21st inst., by a stray shot from a highway robber's pistol. The robber was being closely pushed by the police and used his weapon with the above result.

JACOB SEILLER, of Maumee, Mich., was found dead in the town of Grafton, Laramie county, O., on the night of the 21st ult., with two bullet holes over his right ear and some stabs in his side. Evidently a case of murder.

JOHN ATKINSON, boss herder at the Rosalind agency, D. T., was killed in a row on the 16th inst., by Daniel Gallinan.

South Carolina Bull-Dozing.
From the Phila. Press..

Please allow me space enough in your widely circulated paper to give your readers and the public generally a faint sketch of the unlawful treatment the colored Republicans are now undergoing in this county since the grand Garfield and Arthur ratification meeting, which took place here on the 27th of July. The Democrats tried in every way possible to prevent the colored people from attending the meeting; but they would not be persuaded, and so we we had quite an enthusiastic meeting, between five and six thousand colored between five and si
to order out a sufficient number of men to work on and repair the different public roads for three days, work to commence on the 28th of July. Now, when when the County Commissioners, or sub-Commissioners, Warners found out there was to be a Republican ratification meeting meeting on the 27th of July they changed the order from the 28th to the 26th. (By which one one of these so-called officer's authority it was changed / officer's authority it was changed / am unable to say ) But, however, it was changed, and about twenty-five out of four or five hundred were notified of the change. The others, who never knew of any change taking place, prepared to begin taking place, prepared to begin the work on the 28th instant. No notice of any change appeared in either of the county Democratic papers. And now now they are arresting them from $10 to $15 or putting them them in jail from fifteen to thirty days. They have have extorted out of these poor people already from two to three hundred dollars. Besides this, many have to remain in prison, leaving their wives and little suffering children at home. And God only knows how many are laying out in the woods and swamps to prevent being arrested. And again, after the majority of these poor men returned home, they, the next morning (the 28th). went to the several places of appointment to work the roads and the sub-Commissioners objected to their working, and on returning home to their families many were discharged and driven from off the farms on which they were working. (Many of these people were also working for shares of the crop.) Other colored men who are farming on their own land were visited by a band of these armed midnight riders, and they cursed and abused and threatened and also warned them never to attend another Garfield Republican meeting.

And now, Mr. Editor, I wish you had been among us on Monday or Tuesday to see the colored ministers traveling across the country trying to raise money enough to release their church brethren from imprisonment. I could write you hundreds of pages, for every hour in the day I am receiving divers complaints from different sections and from the officers of the different Garfield and Arthur Clubs in the county of the unlawful treatment they are receiving on account of their politics. But as I only asked for a small space I will close by saying that through all the treatment they have or may receive they are determined to cast their votes for Garfield and Arthur.

Very respectfully yours,

FREDERICK NIX, JR.,
Co Chair'n of the Republican Party of Barnwell Co.

Blackville, S. C., Aug 11, '80.

Democratic clubs in Edgefield, Barnwell, and Hampton, and other counties have adopted resolutions to employ no man, white or colored, who does not support the Democratic nominee; that by reason of this a large number of colored families are now homeless, actually suffering for food, and practically outlawed. MACOUPIN COUNTY.

Gilbert, of this city, addressed a large and enthusiastic audience at Chesterfield. The Hon. B. F. Cowan, candidate for Representative, of Virlen, addressed the Republicans of Brighton in a lengthy address. One of the principal features of the meeting was the torch-light procession comprised of the several Garfield and Arthur clubs.

PERPETUAL MOTION.—Joyce, the colored stone mason of whom we have spoken several times, reports his machine still in motion, and that it has been on the go for 12 months or more without aid or assistance of any kind. He is afraid to let any one see his contrivance for fear the idea will be stolen, and offers the apparatus to any person who will give him $100,000. Joyce is of an ingenious turn of mind and may have discovered some new power, but we wager that at such an exhorbitant price applicants will be few, and lock and key will keep hid from the world his "idea of perpetual motion" for an indeterminate length of time.

HORRIBLE AFFAIR IN DAVIE COUNTY.—Report has reached Winston of a bloody affair that occurred in Jerusalem Township, Davie County, a few nights since. Several rumors are afloat, and we give the most reliable. It appears that a Mr. Phelps who keeps a bar-room had some difficulty with several colored men, and in the fracas shot at them. Not knowing the damage done and fearing an attack during the night he asked a young man by the name of O. K. Click, living near by, to spend the night with him and render assistance if necessary, which request was granted. During the night, however, Click, who is said to be a sombullist, rose and seizing an axe near by attacked Paelps, and in a shorter space of time than it takes to tell it, severed Phelps' head from his body. He awoke about the time the bloody deed was accomplished, horrified at the sight, and is at present said to be almost crazed at the part he took in this unfortunate affair.

At the request of Rev. C. H. Wiley, we publish the following:

Died. At the Merchant's Hotel, in Winston, on the 8th inst., JANE GLENN, colored, aged about 34 years. The deceased was a native of Guilford county, and for some 15 years was a constant member of the Presbyterian Church. She lived several years in the writer's family, was taught to read and write by Mrs. W., and by her industry, integrity and fidelity established for herself a high character among all her acquaintances, white and colored. She read the Bible diligently. She enjoyed the confidence of all who employed her, and her memory is cherished in every family in which she lived. Wherever she was hired she was regarded as a friend, and tho' her last illness was brief and painful, and her summons sudden, her friends have the consolation of believing that she departed in the faith of the Gospel. This is her high praise, this her memorial among all who knew her. She was faithful.

July 31st, 1880.

JOINT MEETING OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS AND JUSTICES OF THE PEACE.—The Board of County Commissioners met at the Court House on Monday, and a considerable portion of the morning session was spent in allowing paupers claims, releases from Poll tax and other unimportant business. It being the day for the assembling of the Justices of the Peace in a joint session with the Board, they assembled, 28 responding to the roll call. This being a majority of the Justices of the Peace in the county, they proceeded to transact the following business:

Ordered that a tax of 25 cents be levied on the $100 valuation of real and personal property, and 75 cents on each taxable poll for county purposes, and also the same under schedule B., as levied by the State for State purposes.

Decided that 5 cents additional Stock law tax be levied on $100 valuation of real estate, situated in those townships which have adopted the Stock Law.

event-1880-08-01.A2:
A SOMNAMBULIST'S MURDER.
Horrible Death of a Merchant at the Hands of a Sleep-Walker. [Charlotte (N. C.) Observer.]
[Charlotte (N. C.) Observer.]
Tyro a little village in Davi

At Tyro, a little village in Davidson county, Mr. Uriah Phelps has a store. A few nights since he had a difficulty with some negroes whom he and his brother had attempted to eject from the house. Anticipating a further difficulty with the negroes, he secured the services of Mr. O. W. Click, a young man who lives in the neighborhood, and who is in the habit of walking in his sleep. They lay in the store and watched for half the night, and finally fell asleep, having stretched themselves across the bed.

It appears from subsequent developments that Click, the somnambulist, got up, and, seizing an axe that had been placed near the bed, to be used in case of an emergency, dealt his bed-fellow two blows across the neck, completely severing the head from the body. Click is now in custody, awaiting the result of the coroner's inquest. He professes to have known nothing of the occurrence until some time after the deed was committed, and even denied that he did it until convinced by the overwhelming testimony of the blood-stained weapon and the condition of his garments, together with the fact that there was no one else in the room, and no evidence that any one could by any means have entered and afterwards gone out without disturbing the locks and bars.

The case has naturally caused considerable excitement in the community. Click's well-known habit of sleep-walking, together with the friendly relations which had existed between the two men, turn the scale of public opinion in his favor. The result of the coroner's investigation and the preliminary trial is awaited with interest.

event-1880-08-01.A7:
A PRELIMINARY HEARING OF THE CASE OF THE SLEEPING MURDERER AND HIS DISCHARGE FROM CUSTODY.

[Charlotte (N. C.) Observer.]

Information from Tyro, the scene of the recent somnambulistic murder, is that over a hundred people assembled at the coroner's inquest and preliminary trial. The body of Mr. Phelps was found lying nearly across the foot of the bed, on the right side, his head on his right arm, with three cuts with an axe, two of which, if not the third, were sufficient to cause instant death—one high enough on the head to reach the brain.

The story of Mr. Click was that he dreamed the negroes had entered the store as anticipated by himself and Mr. Phelps. There followed, according to his recollection, a bloody and terrible fight. When he awoke he was fleeing down the stairs, and gradually recovering consciousness, he returned to the room where he and Phelps had been sleeping, and realized at a glance the full horror of his deed. He at once fled, screaming, to the house of Mr. Grub, near by, and was met by that gentleman, who had been aroused by his cries. Mr. Grub said his lamentations were heartrending, and that he told him at once that he had killed his best friend in his sleep. The alarm soon became general, and the neighbors collected from all quarters. They all testified that Click exhibited in a most violent manner his regret, and finally became so exhausted that he had to be carried home.

The preliminary trial was had before Justices Thompson and Hartley, and Messrs. Clement and Bailey, of Mocksville, and Mr. H. Pinnix, of Lexington, appeared for the defendant. It was proved by both State and defendant's witnesses that Click was a somnambulist and had frequently injured his own person by jumping from the house window—sometimes through the glass from the second story, cutting himself considerably. He has also been known to get up and choke some of the family, saying that the bears in Texas were after him; and then run a quarter or a half mile down near the river, and wake to find himself alone. When he went visiting he requested his neighbors to tie him, which they did. Last week he went to sleep in the room where his dead uncle lay a corpse. He suddenly arose with terrible expressions of fear and started to seize his dead uncle. His sister and a gentleman caught him, got him awake, and he went back to bed. Many other instances were given. Mr. Clement addressed the court in an impressive manner, setting forth the law in such cases and showing conclusively that a somnambulist was not accountable for his acts while unconscious. He was followed by Mr. H. Pinnix in a short and pointed speech. The Court being satisfied from the evidence that the prisoner was not accountable for his actions while asleep, pronounced the evidence insufficient; whereupon Mr. Click returned to his home.

shelbyville-shelbyville-1880-08.A3:
Intimidation in Indiana.
thought
CINCINNATI, August 12.—Demeratic threats of driving the negroes out of Indiana are being put into execution in at least three counties.

Early yesterday morning a band of masked Kuklux attacked the house of an inoffensive negro named Joshua Mack, one mile from Columbus, Ind., broke open the door and windows, and dragged him from his bed, declaring with vile oaths that they would hang him, and that they intended to "clean out all the niggers in the county before the election." They ransacked the house for arms, and found none, and finally agreed to let Mack go on condition that he would immediately leave. After they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others of the party were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after the house of Mr. Walker, who has a farm rented on which the negro lives, was stoned, the party yelling, cursing, and threatening about it for a considerable time. At Bluffton and Shelbyville similar attempts at intimidation have been made.

thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A1:
RIOT IN COFFEEVILLE, MISS. The Greenback Candidate for Sheriff Shooting a Democratic Negro.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 22.—From passengers who arrived this morning the following particulars have been gained of a riot which occurred yesterday in Coffeeville, Miss., the county seat of Yallabusha County. A special election is to be held next Tuesday to fill a vacancy in the Sheriff's office, over which there was a contest at the last general election. The Democrats and Greenbackers have each a ticket in the field. Both parties held a ratification meeting at Coffeeville on Saturday. Each raised a pole. The Democrats had a brass band from Grenada, and after the pole-raising marched through the streets.

While passing a corner a difficulty occurred between a negro named Spearman, who was in the Democratic procession, and A. V. Pearson, Greenback candidate for Sheriff, which resulted in Pearson shooting Spearman, killing him instantly. This was the signal for a general melée, and a volley of shots was opened on Pearson, who received three wounds, from the effects of which he died last night. Two of Pearson's friends, Kelly and Reddick, were wounded. For a time a perfect pandemonium reigned, the excitement running so high that the Walthall Grays, a military company of Grenada, Miss., were telegraphed for, but the order was subsequently countermanded. Last night Coffeeville was quiet.
thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A2:
FATAL POLITICAL FIGHT.
There has been a serious political riot at Coffeeeville, Miss. A special election for Sheriff is to be held there to-morrow, and the Democrats and Greenbackers have each a candidate in the field. Both parties held ratification meetings and raised flag poles on Saturday, and after their pole raising the Democrats, headed by a brass band from Grenada, paraded through the streets. While passing a corner, a difficulty arose between a negro named Spearman, who was in the Democratic parade, and A. V. V. Pearson, the Greenback candidate for Sheriff. Pearson shot Spearman dead on the spot, and a general fight ensued, in which Pearson and two of his friends were wounded, Pearson dying of his wounds at night. A military company was telegraphed to come from Grenada to put put down down the riot, but the disorder subsiding, the order was subsequently countermanded.
thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A4:
AN UNNOTICED OUTRAGE..
An election was held in Yalabusha county, Mississippi, yesterday for sheriff, to fill a vacancy. There were two tickets in the field, the Democrat and the Fusion, the latter supported by Republicans and Greenbackers. The county in 1876 gave Tilden 1,904 votes and Hayes 831. On a straight party vote the Democrats outnumbered the Republicans over two to one; so the only hope for the latter to elect their candidate for sheriff was based on fusing with the Greenbackers and drawing heavily from the Democratic ranks. Last Saturday the Democrats and the Fusionists held ratification meetings at Coffeeville, the county seat. Both parties marched through the streets and in passing a corner a col-
streets, and in passing a corner a col- ered man in the Democratic ranks ran against the Fusion candidate for sheriff. The would-be sheriff drew a pistol and shot the negro instantly. This was the signal for a melee, in which several shots were fired, and two white men, friends of the candidate for sheriff, were wounded. The Associated Press calls this a political riot, but had the colored man been a Republican instead of a Democrat, the partisan news gather- ers would have styled it a southern outrage. Then the whole Republican press with one accord would have waived the bloody shirt and endeavored to fire the northern heart. As it is they pass it unnoticed as something unworthy of special mention, because the victim was a colored Democrat.

The situation just now recalls a circumstance which occurred in Mississippi in 1874. Governor Ames aspired to the United States Senate, and desired to create some political as well as personal capital. His competitor for the senatorial prize was ex-Governor Alcorn, also a Republican. J. Wiley Wells, who was since elected to Congress and stumped California for Hayes four years ago was District Attorney in one of the most populous counties in what is called "The black belt," of Mississippi. He testified before a Congressional investigating committee appointed in the winter of 1864-5. of which we believe
would result in rioting and bloodshed. "Never mind," said the Governor, "the blood of fifteen or twenty negroes, killed for political purposes, would do me and the party heaps of good, if it could be made to appear that they were killed by southern shot-guns because of their political opinions. It is a sad commentary on the degeneracy of the Republican party, which was founded by statesmen on pure principles, that its modern leaders, many of whom were secessionists in the early days of the war, rely exclusively for success in the present campaign on the "bloody shirt."
thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A8:
The Coffeeville Slot.
FURTHER PARTICULARS OF THE AFFAIR
HOW IT BEGAN AND THE RESULT
OF THE ROW.
Coffeeville, Miss., Aug. 22.—Yesterday, the twenty-first, was the day set apart at Coffeeville for the grand ratification meeting and flag-raising by the Democratic party at Yallabusha county. Early in the morning crowds poured into the town from all parts of the country. The Democratic clubs had expected to have their speakers in the court-house, and the first bad feeling was caused by the Greenbackers taking charge of the court-house and holding speaking there.

To prevent any trouble the Democrats retired to a wood near the place, although it had been announced and was understood that their speaking would be held at the court-house. Col. W. H. Fizgerald, of Grenada, and Capt. Walter M. Jackson, of Water Valley, addressed the Democratic clubs in the woods, and S. A. Harmon held forth to the Greenbackers at the court-house. The speaking of both parties terminated about three o'clock. The Democratic clubs then marched through town, headed by the Grenada band, and were met on Depot street by the Greenback clubs, when, from some unknown reason, B. V. Pearson's, Greenback candidate for sheriff, struck and shot Thos. Spearman, a colored man, who was marching with the Democrats.

This caused the men marching in the front rank to take part in the affray, and for a while the wildest excitement ensued. The negroes fled like scared sheep in all directions, and, in less time than it takes to tell it, every store-house in the town was closed and the streets swarmed with armed men. Pearson's was shot three times, one ball in the shoulder and two in the legs. After falling he was carried into an adjacent store and given medical attention. His wounds are necessarily fatal. Thos. Spearman, the negro, was shot in the neck by Pearson's. His whereabouts are not known. R. B. Riddick was painfully wounded in the thigh; R. C. Kelly only slightly. Gov. Stone and Secretary of State Henry C. Meyers were in town to-day. Gov. Stone complimented Capt. R. H. Wyatt, commanding the Coffeeville Guards, and Mayor Ross on their action in the matter. The Democrats will hold another meeting here to-morrow, and the election for sheriff will take place Tuesday.
thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A9:
THE COFFEEVILLE AFFAIR.
A Correct Report.
The following particulars of the origin of the difficulty at Coffeeville, we copy from the Memphis Appeal. The report is endorsed by Gov. Stone, and Hon. H. C. Myers, who were at Coffeeville recently, as a correct report of the affair, as given by those who were present at the time of the troubles:

COFFEEVILLE, Aug. 22,—A street fight occurred here last evening, in which four persons were wounded and fears were entertained for a time that the whole town would become involved. The difficulty originated between R. V. Pearson, the Greenback candidate for Sheriff, and W. T. Spearman, colored, the Republican election commissioner for this county. A Democratic ratification meeting and pole-raising was in progress, having been appointed several weeks previous. The day before the Greenback leaders sent out runners, and held a meeting the same time the Democratic ratification meeting was being held. The speaking had closed and a Democratic procession was marching through the streets when Pearson made the attack on Spearman. Several shots were exchanged, and Pearson was seriously and Spearman slightly wounded. R. B. Ridgick, and B. C. Kelly, who were marching at the head of the Democratic procession, were innocently drawn into the difficulty, and both received slight wounds. A high state of excitement prevailed for a time, but quiet was soon restored. Under the existing excitement telegrams were sent to Governor Stone, who, with Captain Myers, Secretary of State, came up on the first train and found everything quiet. They will return to the capital on this evening's train, perfectly assured that there is no danger of further trouble. There is considerable political excitement in this county, in consequence of the special election for sheriff, to be held on Tuesday, the twenty-fourth instant. The Democrats of the county deplore the difficulty of yesterday, and are doing everything in their power to have a peaceable and fair election.

Spearman's letter hereto appended will explain the cause of the difficulty.

SPEARMAN'S CARD.

COFFEEVILLE, MISS.,

August 19, 1880.
EDITOR CENTRAL:

SIR—I take this method of setting myself right before the people of Yalobusha county. I address this letter most especially to the colored people of this county. I am not in the habit of resorting to printer's ink to vindicate my character. I am charged by men who belong to the Greenback party of having sold myself, or rather have been bought by the Democratic party. These charges are brought against me because I have seen fit to announce my intention to vote for the Republican candidates for President and Vice President. I further announce my intention of voting for Jennings for Sheriff, and any charge that may be brought against me as having sold out to the Democratic party I denounce as being utterly false, without even the slightest semblance of truth. I advise all men, irrespective of past political party affiliations, that want to see the bitterness of feeling engendered by the political muddle that has disgraced Yalobusha for the past six months to vote for Jennings, as I believe him to be the man entit'ed to the support of all good men. I hope the people of Yalobusha county will understand my position. I am going to support the Republican candidates for President and Vice-President, and Buchanan for Congress, if I am the only man in this county that votes for them; and besides I expect to do all I can to organize the party. My fellow-citizens, consider well the condition of our county, and vote intelligently for Jennings for heriff. In conclusion let me say to my people (the colored people), when you are met with the charge that I have been bought by Democracy, I authorize you to denounce it a malicious, slanderous and unconditional falsehood. Very respectfully,
W. T. SPEARMAN.

thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A14:
A Nearly Dead Greenbacker Elected Sheriff.
The associated press dispatches last week stated that R. V. Pearson, greenback nominee for sheriff of Yalobusha county, Mississippi, shot and killed a democratic negro. The facts as we glean them from a Mississippi exchange, are as follows: There was a special election for sheriff, near at hand; Pearson was almost sure to be elected; for some unknown reason, he was accosted by a republican negro, who, however, was wearing a democratic badge; a quarrel ensued and Pearson struck the negro with his umbrella; the negro ran across the street and shot back at Pearson, and some say Pearson returned the fire, but the negro ran around a corner and was out of danger.

A few seconds elapsed when Pearson was fired upon by a procession of democrats, two of the shots taking effect in his legs. Pearson turned and fired at the mob sightly wounding one man. When Pearson turned on the crowd a man in front of him fired at him. Pearson turned on him, and they exchanged several shots, Pearson receiving a navy ball in his right lung and his assailant, a slight wound.

It is thought that there was a deep laid scheme to murder Pearson.

These are the facts about "a greenbacker's killing an innocent colored democrat," as charged by Mr. Kinley Saturday.

VOTERS, while the democratic press and politicians are lying about the greenback party, and slandering the working people, don't let it escape your notice that the democratic party with full power in congress, obtained under the most solemn promises to reform and undo the unjust and robbing legislation of the republican party, has refused and failed to pass or attempt to pass a single solitary act toward the fulfillment of their promises. The democratic congress was in session for months with hundreds of millions of gold and silver dollars lying hoarded in the treasury, and would not direct one dollar of them to be used in paying bonds and thus lighten the burden which rests so heavily on the country. Remember too, that when a resolution was introduced declaring that the bonds which fall due next year should not be refunded beyond the power of the government to pay them at anytime, but should be paid as rapidly as possible according to contract, the democratic congress defeated that resolution.

Read the democratic platform and post yourselves as to the proceedings of the recent session of congress and you will find that the democratic party, or rather the leaders thereof, have sold out body and soul to the money power.

R. W. SPEARMAN, a colored man, late of Yalobusha county, writes as follows to Capt. Brown of the Mississippi Central, under date of Fort Scott, Kansas, September 12, 1880:

DEAR SIR: The Greenback mob has driven me from my home in the Sunny South for no other reason than that I advocated the principles of the Republican party, and supported Jennings for sheriff.
thos-spear-coffeeville-1880-08-21.A17:
A serious difficulty occurred between the Greenhackers and Democrats at Coffeeville
A serious difficulty occurred between the Greenbackers and Democrats at Coffeeville, Yalobusha county, Miss., on the 21st of last month, of which A. T. Wimberly, chairman of the Greenback State committee, gives a lengthy account in the Yalobusha Standard. His version of the affair is that the Democrats hired a colored man named Spearman to proclaim himself a Republican, hoping that he would injure the Greenback party by resurrecting the Republican organization. Failing in that, he picked a quarrel with the Greenback candidate for sheriff, on the 21st, when the Greenbackers and Democrats had assembled for a joint discussion. The colored man insulted the Greenbacker as he was passing along the street. The Greenbacker punched the colored man with an umbrella, whereupon the colored man and a half dozen Democrats drew revolvers and shot the Greenbacker down. Some of the men who fired the shots he considered his personal friends; in fact, he said he did not know that he had an enemy in the world. Two days after, the Democrats from that and adjoining counties came in with their knives, guns and pistols, they said, to keep the peace. Among their other peaceful demonstrations was to send a committee to Mr. Wimberly, asking him to cease advocating the Greenback cause or die before midnight. Mr. Wimberly refused their articles of peace, and another committee was sent, demanding from him an unconditional surrender of his political principles. One of the committee was secretary of his lodge, the Forresters. Mr. Wimberly settled his dues, that his family might obtain his insurance money without any trouble, and then requested that he might be shot by a committee of five, in army style, but not by a mob. However, his life has been spared so far, and he thinks it will be for some time to come.

Governor Stone visited the place the day before the Democrats flocked in to keep the peace. Mr. Wimberly waited upon the Governor and informed him of the coming trouble. He suggested that the military act under the order of the civil authorities, which consisted of men of both parties. He believed that if it would go out that the Governor demanded peace there would be no trouble. The Governor could not see that he had any power to act; besides, prominent Democrats informed him that there would be no trouble. The Governor put himself in the hands of the politicians, and made no move to prevent trouble.

Mr. Wimberly says if they attempt bulldozing there will be trouble. He fought in the confederate army from the first to the last, believing it a just cause, and now he is just as ready to die in this cause. Mississippi is his home and he intends to live and move there. In conclusion he says:

"I have heard and read of these things, said to have been committed in the South, and must confess that I did not believe half that I heard, and the only reason that I can assign is that I was a member of the Democratid party, and like hundreds and thousands of others who are now members of the same party, blinded to its corruption and incapability of controlling anything but a mob. In 1861, when Wm. L. Yancy, in Memphis, made his noted secession speech, I was standing near my father, who looked at me and said: 'My son, if that policy is carried out, and Democracy is upheld, it will be the damnation of the South.' I, in the language of my father, say if Democracy gets control of this government, it will be the destruction of the liberties of the people. God, let the heavens fall, let the earth sink, let the sun cease to shine; but for mercy's sake, and for the sake of the rising generation, crush the so-called Democracy, is my honest and earnest prayer."

The large bulk of Southern men, the same as at the North, desire only what is for the best interests of the nation. The office-seekers, the same as North, adopt vicious means of holding power, but, the same as here, prejudice has blinded the people to a true state of affairs. Such men as Mr. Wimberly understand the disease, and know the remedy, and have the nerve to apply it. Northern interference excites prejudice and will prolong the trouble.

winnsborough-winnsborough-1880-07.A1:
—In Franklin Parish, La., on Fri
In Franklin Parish, La., on Friday two weeks ago, a negro boy aged seventeen, attempted to outrage a young lady, daughter of a prominent lawyer of that Parish. We extract the following from a dispatch to the New Orleans Times: "He got into her room through a window, and got in her bed before she discovered him. Her screams awoke her father, when the negro jumped from the window, making his escape for the time. He was soon captured by the Sheriff and lodged in jail. He confessed to the fact, and also that in the past twelve months he had attempted to enter almost every house in Winnsborough. About 12 o'clock Saturday night a body of men went to the jail, broke off the lock, took him out and hung him to a tree about 100 yards from town, where he was found hanging Sunday morning."
